number_of_offences: Charged under sections 406, 420 and 417 IPC; upheld under sections 420 and 406
key_evidence_accepted: The Court accepted that the dispute arose from a loan transaction and that the respondent had instituted a summary civil suit for recovery, which is still pending adjudication.
witness_credibility: The Court did not assess the credibility of the main witnesses directly but noted that there was no dishonest representation or inducement shown in the complaint or material.
bail_history: The appellant was enlarged on bail by the High Court after being arrested on 29.01.2012.

trial_duration.trial_judgment: The High Court dismissed the quashing petition and directed the trial court to complete the trial within three months.
trial_duration.high_court_decision: The High Court observed that prima facie an offence of cheating under s.420 was made out but charge under s.406 was not applicable.
trial_duration.supreme_court_decision: The Supreme Court quashed the proceedings initiated based on the FIR and allowed the appeal.

legal_representation.accused: Praveen Kumar Rai, Hemal Kiritkumar Sheth
legal_representation.state: I. H. Syed, Varinder Kumar Sharma, Ms. Puja, Ms. Vishakha, Ms. Parul Luthra (for Ms. Hemantika Wahi)

investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
procedural_irregularity: The appellant alleged that the charges were framed without giving him an opportunity of being heard, as he was unaccompanied by any counsel.

appeal_history.trial_court: The Trial Court framed charges against the appellant.
appeal_history.high_court: The High Court dismissed the quashing petition and directed the trial court to complete the trial.
appeal_history.supreme_court: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and quashed the proceedings initiated based on the FIR.

prosecution_argument: The State argued that the appellant had obtained a loan from a money lending company, failed to repay it, and threatened the respondent with dire consequences, thereby constituting an offence under Sections 406, 420, and 417 of the IPC.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the allegations were civil in nature, there was no clear case of entrustment, and the mere breach of a promise or contract does not constitute the offence of criminal breach of trust or cheating without fraudulent or dishonest intention.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that a mere breach of a promise, agreement, or contract does not constitute the offence of criminal breach of trust or cheating without a clear case of entrustment or fraudulent intention.
precedent_relied_upon: State of Bihar v. Ramesh Singh 1977 CriLJ 1606; Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma v. State of Bihar (2000) 4 SCC 168; Gian Singh v. State of Punjab (2012) 10 SCC 303
